fr:mainmatter.html:p: The set of complex numbers \mathbb {C} is not compact, but we can compactify it, just like we can do so with the real line \R (which is also not compact).

One way to compactify \R is to add to it a point at infinity and obtain the set \overline {\R } = \R \cup \{\infty \} -- this is called the one-point compactification (distinguishing between \pm \infty yields the so called two-point compactification). Turns out, \overline \R is homeomorphic to a circle in the Euclidean plane, thus, the unit circle is a nice tangible model of \overline \R . If we put a circle on top of the real line, and let it touch the line at 0, and if we stereographically project (in 2D sense) all the points of the circle onto the line, we can get a 1-1 correspondence between all the points of the circle and the real line, except for one: the antipodal point of 0, which we call the north pole; for this \R won't do, but \overline \R will.

We can compactify \mathbb {C} in a similar manner: just do \overline {\mathbb {C}} = \mathbb {C} \cup \{\infty \}. A tangible model for this compactification is a sphere, also usually called the Riemann sphere. Conventions may vary, but we can think of it as a sphere placed on the complex plane, touching the xy-plane at (0,0,0), centered at (0,0,1), with a radius of 1. Then the north pole N is at the point (0,0,2). The reason why the Riemann sphere is indeed a model of (ie. homeomorphic to) \overline {\mathbb {C}} is again the stereographic projection; in order to map the north pole N somewhere, \mathbb {C} alone won't do, but in \overline {\mathbb {C}}, N has a natural place to map to: \infty .

We can define a metric \rho on \overline {\mathbb {C}} for complex numbers s_1, s_2 in the following way: \rho (s_1,s_2) = \overline {S_1 S_2}, where S_1, S_2 are points on the Riemann sphere corresponding to s_1, s_2.
With such metric, \overline {\mathbb {C}} is compact, whereas the plain \mathbb {C} was only locally compact (and unbounded) wrt. to the usual metric.

A set D \subseteq \mathbb {C} that is both open and connected is called a domain.
We say that a domain U is simply connected if the set \mathbb {C}\setminus U has no bounded components. In other words, it's a domain with no holes.
A useful characterisation is the theorem that says that U is simply connected iff \overline {\mathbb {C}} \setminus U is connected.
A domain that's not simply connected is a multiply connected domain; i.e. it has holes.

A continuous curve in the complex plane is the image of a continuous complex mapping \gamma : [\alpha , \beta ] \to \mathbb {C}. It can be described with the equation: \gamma (t) = x(t) + iy(t), \quad t \in [\alpha , \beta ] where x, y are continuous real functions of t \in [\alpha , \beta ].
A curve has an orientation: for a positively oriented curve \gamma , we denote the same curve with clockwise orinetation with -\gamma .
A Jordan (or simple) curve \gamma is a curve that has no self-intersections.

A continuous curve \gamma in the complex plane is smooth if it can be parametrised with t \in [\alpha , \beta ] with a continuously-differentiable mapping, whose derivative has no zeroes for t \in [\alpha , \beta ].
A piecewise smooth curve is a curve that is made of finitely many smooth curves. More idiomatically, we call such a curve a contour.
Here are some key results regarding these basic notions.
If K \subset \mathbb {C} is compact, then \mathbb {C} \setminus K has exactly one unbounded component.
A domain U is simply connected iff \overline {\mathbb {C}} \setminus U is connected.
Every open convex subset of \mathbb {C} is a simply connected domain.
Every simple closed curve \gamma \subset \mathbb {C} divides \mathbb {C} in two disjoint domains, of which one is bounded and the other unbounded; \gamma is the boundary of both those domains.
For a curve \gamma : I \to \mathbb {C} in \mathbb {C} and \varepsilon >0 there always exists a piecewise linear curve \tilde \gamma s.t. d(\gamma ,\tilde \gamma )<\varepsilon .
In other words, we can approximate every curve with a piecewise linear curve to an arbitrary precision.

Let f be a complex function that's defined on some open disk that contains the point z_0. We say that f is analytic (or differentiable) in z_0, if the following limit exists in \mathbb {C}: \lim _{z \to z_0}\frac {f(z)-f(z_0)}{z-z_0}
Function f is holomorphic on a domain U, if it's differentiable (analytic) in a neighborhood of every point of the domain U.
Let f(z) = u(x,y) + iv(x,y), for x+iy = z \in D\subseteq \mathbb {C}, where D is open; let also (x_0,y_0) = z_0 \in D.

html:ol.html:li: If f is differentiable in z_0, then the first order partial derivatives of functions u,v in point z_0 exist and they satisfy the equations u'_x = v'_y, u'_y = - v'_x. If f is analytic in z_0 and f'(z_0) is continuous, then the partial derivatives of u,v wrt. to x,y are continuous.

Suppose u,v have first order partial derivatives in some neighborhood of z_0, and suppose those are continuous funcitons in z_0, s.t. the PDEs (C-R equations) above hold. Then function f is differentiable in z_0.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Immediate corollary: If f doesn't satisfy C-R equations in z_0 = (x_0, y_0), then f is not differentiable in that point.
A geometric interpretation of C-R equations tells us that the gradients of multivariable functions u,v are orthogonal, if they satisfy C-R.

A function u of two real variables is harmonic if it has partial derivatives of first and second order, which are continuous functions, and if it satisfies the Laplace equation in \R ^2: \frac {\partial ^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \frac {\partial ^2 u}{\partial y^2} = 0.

fr:title.text: Real&imaginary functions of holomorphic functions are harmonic

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Real&imaginary functions of holomorphic functions are harmonic

fr:mainmatter.html:p: If the function f = u+iv is holomorphic on an open set D, then the functions u and v are harmonic. (Proof is immediate from the C-R theorem.)

If u is harmonic on domain D and v is harmonic s.t. u+iv is holomorphic, then we say that v is the harmonic conjugate of u. (v is unique up to an additive constant; the next theorem gives us information about existence.)
If D is a simply connected domain, and u harmonic on D, then there exists a(the) harmonic conjugate of u.

Power series are important, thus the spoiler: every function that's analytic in some neighborhood has a power series representation, i.e. it can be written as a power series (in that neighborhood). This also sheds some light on why the functions that are locally representable by a power series are also called analytic (in broader sense; if you thought the overloaded, it kind of isn't.)
Let \sum _{n}^{\infty } f_n be a series of continuous functions on an open set D\subseteq \mathbb {C} that converges uniformly to f on D. Then f is continuous on D.
A power series is a series of the form \sum _{n=0}^{\infty } a_n (z-z_0)^n where a_n is a sequence in C and z_0 \in \mathbb {C} is an arbitrary point.
By setting w = z-z_0, we can write the series like \sum _{n=0}^{\infty } a_n w^n and we often use this shortcut to talk about power series, by assuming wlog. that z_0 = 0.

Let f be a power series as in the above definition and let L := \limsup \limits _{n \to \infty } \sqrt [n]{|a_n|}.
If L = 0, then the power series f converges for all z \in \mathbb {C}.
If L = \infty , then the power series f converges only for z = z_0.
If L \in (0,\infty ), then the power series f converges for |z-z_0|<R, and diverges for |z-z_0| > R, where R = 1/L.
It's immediate that a convergent power series converges absolutely within the disk D(z_0, R).

The above theorem doesn't give us information whether the power series converges on the boundary (circle) |z-z_0| = R; it's possible that the series converges only for some points on the boundary, and also that it converges/diverges for every point on the boundary.
The R=1/L defined in the theorem above is called the radius of convergence of the given power series.
Let R \in 0, \lparen \infty \rbrack , then the power series converges uniformly on every closed disk \bar {D}(z_0, R_{\delta }), where R_{\delta }=R-\delta for any \delta \in (0, R).
An immediate corollary of this is that the power series as a function is continuous on D(z_0, R).
As we saw, the power series is a series whose terms are functions of the form f_n(z):=a_n(z-z_0)^n which are holomorphic on the whole complex plane and whose derivative is f_{n}'= na_n(z-z_0)^{n-1}.
Now we are going to focus on the results that say that the power series is a holomorphic function within the disk of convergence, and that we can differentiate the series term by term.

fr:title.text: Series of derivatives has same radius of convergence

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Series of derivatives has same radius of convergence

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let the power series f(z) = \sum _{n=0}^{\infty } a_n z^n have a radius of convergence R, then the series of derivatives g(z) = \sum _{n=1}^{\infty } na_n z^{n-1} also has radius of convergence R.

fr:title.text: Power series is a holomorphic function within disk of convergence

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Power series is a holomorphic function within disk of convergence

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let f(z) be as in above, and R its radius of convergence. Then f is holomorphic on D(0,R) and we have f'(z) = \sum _{n=1}^{\infty } n a_n z^{n-1}. In other words, we can differentiate the power series term by term.
This easily generalizes to the more general shifted power series whose terms are a_n(z-z_0)^{n-1}.

fr:title.text: A power series is inifinitely differentiable in D

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A power series is inifinitely differentiable in D

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let f be a power series and R its radius of convergence. Then f is differentiable for every k \in \mathbb N in every point z \in D(z_0, R) and the following holds: f^{(k)}(z) = \sum _{n=k}^{\infty } n(n-1)\dots (n-(k-1))a_n(z-z_0)^{n-k}. (proof by induction)

Let f(z) := \sum _{n=0}^{\infty }a_n(z-z_0)^n, \quad g(z):= \sum _{n=0}^{\infty }b_n(z-z_0)^n \ , be two power series that are convergent for all z \in D(z_0, R). Let \{w_k\} \subseteq D(z_0, R) be a sequence of complex numbers s.t. \lim _{k \to \infty }w_k = z_0 but w_k \neq z_0 for all k \in \mathbb {N}. If f(w_k) = g(w_k) for all k, then a_n = b_n for all n\geq 0, that is, f(z) = g(z) for all z \in D(z_0, R).
In other words, if two convergent power series are equal on an countable set of elements of the complex plane, then they are equal (everywhere else).

There are two important elementary functions, from which other elementary functions, like trigonometric, hyperbolic or power functions can be defined. Those two functions are the exponential function and the logarithm.
The function e^z: \mathbb {C} \to \mathbb {C} (or \text {exp}(z)) is defined as the value of the following convergent power series: e^z := \sum _{n=0}^{\infty }\frac {z^n}{n!} \ .
The complex exponential function has the same properties as its real counterpart.

Based on what we said earlier, it's easy to see that e^z is holomorphic on \mathbb {C} and that (e^z)' = e^z for all z \in \mathbb {C}. It's also the only such function, ie. the only function for which f'(z) = f(z) and f(0) = 1 holds, and this can be used as an equivalent definition of the exponential function, namely, we can define it for all z \in \mathbb {C} as e^z : = e^x (\cos y + i \sin y).
Let us now observe how the exponential function behaves in the complex plane.
For z \in \mathbb {R}, e^z maps \mathbb {C} to (0, \infty ).

For a fixed y_0, \mathbb {C} \ni z = x + iy_0 is a horizontal line. Let's see to what this line gets mapped to via the exp function. By the division algorithm, we can get y_0 = k\cdot 2\pi + r etc. then we have e^z = e^x e^{ir} = e^x (\cos r + i \sin r), which is a ray from the origin, making an angle of r with the positive real axis.
Consider now a vertical line z = x_0 + iy. We can see that a vertical line gets mapped to a circle of radius e^{x_0}, since e^z = e^{x_0}(\cos y + i \sin y).

It can easily be shown that the exponential is injective on every horizontal strip \{z \in \mathbb {C} : a < \text {Im}(z) \leq a + 2 \pi \} of the complex plane, for any a \in \mathbb {R}, and it maps this strip to the whole complex plane.

From the above we deduce that for a given point w_0 = |w_0|e^{i\text {Arg}(w_0)} of the w-plane there's infinitely many points of the z-plane that map into w_0. Those points are z_k(w_0) = \log (|w_0|) + i\text {Arg}(w_0)+2\pi i k, for any k \in \mathbb {Z}.
We can now move onto the complex logarithm.

The real exponential function is a bijective mapping from \mathbb {R} to (0,\infty ), and as such it had an inverse function, namely the logarithm. However, as we have seen in the last paragraph above, the exponential function is not injective, so it's less clear how we should go about defining the complex logarithm. For starters, we will define it as a multi-valued function, but we will see that from there we can obtain a well behaved "usual" function (by choosing a specific branch of the complex log).

For z \in \mathbb {C} \setminus \{0\} the complex logarithm is defined as a multi-valued function defined with: \ln z = \log |z| + i \text {arg}(z) = i \text {Arg}(z) + 2k\pi i \ , \ k \in \mathbb {Z} \ .

The principal value (or the main branch) of the log function is the single-valued function \text {Log}(z) = \log |z| + i\text {Arg}(z). This is the unique inverse of the exponential map when we restrict it to the horizontal strip \{z \in \mathbb {C} : -\pi < \text {Im}(z) \leq \pi \}.
It follows immediately from the Cauchy-Riemann equations that the principal value is a holomorphic function on \mathbb {C} \setminus \{0\} and its derivative is 1/z.
For example, all values of \log 3 are \ln 3 + 2k\pi i, \ k \in \mathbb {Z}, ie. there's infinitely many of them.
Let's observe how \text {Log}(z) maps the cut z-plane \mathbb {C} \setminus \lparen -\infty , 0 \rbrack on the w-plane.

As we have seen in the exp function section, the ray \text {Arg}(z) = \theta _0 maps to the horizontal line \text {Im}(w) = \theta _0. As \theta _0 varies in (-\pi , \pi ), the corresponding rays fill the whole cut z-plane. Thus the cut z-plane maps via \text {Log}(z) onto the horizontal strip \{w \in \mathbb {C} : -\pi < \text {Im}(w)< \pi \}.
Let's now show how to construct the Riemann surface of the complex log function.

Observe the sequence of functions f_k(z) = w_k = \ln |z| + i \text {Arg}(z) + 2k \pi i, \ k \in \mathbb {Z}, ie. the sequence of the branches of the log function, on the cut z-plane \mathbb {C}\setminus \lparen -\infty , 0 \rbrack . By the same reasoning above as for the main branch f_0, we have that all branches f_k map \mathbb {C} \setminus \lparen -\infty , 0 \rbrack onto the horizontal strip \{w \in \mathbb {C} : 2k\pi - \pi < \text {Im}(w) < 2k\pi + \pi \}. Now for every k \in \mathbb {Z} we can define S_k := \mathbb {C} \setminus \lparen -\infty , 0 \rbrack . Now, we can obtain a surface S by glueing S_k and S_{k-1} along their cuts in the following way: the part above the cut of S_k, ie. the part that's in the strictly positive half-plane we glue to the part below the cut of S_{k-1}, ie. the part that's in the negative half-plane; we proceed inductively for every k. What did we achieve with this? Well, let's look at the following limits for k-th branches: \lim \limits _{z \to r+i0} f_k(z) = \ln |r| + i(2k+1)\pi , \quad \lim \limits _{z \to r-i0} f_k(z) = \ln |r| + i(2k-1)\pi = \lim \limits _{z \to r+i0} f_{k-1}(z). This enables us that the function f(z):S \to \mathbb {C}, \ f(z):= f_k(z) for z \in S_k becomes continuous. Moreover, f(z) = \log z, in the sense that values of f(z) coincide with \log z for points of the surface S that correspond to the complex numbers z. Such constructed surface S is the Riemann surface of the complex logarithm function. Since there's a bijective correspondence between S and \mathbb {C} \setminus \{0\}, this surface can be viewed as a sphere with its points at the north and south poles removed.

For non-principal branches the following identity holds: \log (zw) = \log z + \log w. For the principal branch for all z,w \in \mathbb {C} \setminus \{0\} we have \text {Log}(zw) = \text {Log}(z) + \text {Log}(w) + 2k\pi i, for some k \in \{-1,0,1\}.
Functions \cos z and \sin z are defined for all z \in \mathbb {C} with: \cos z := \frac {1}{2}(e^{iz}+e^{-iz}) \ , \sin z := \frac {1}{2i}(e^{iz}-e^{-iz}) \ .
For example the set of solutions of \sin z = 0 is \{k\pi :k \in \mathbb {Z}\}, and the set of solutions of \cos z = 0 is \{\pi /2 + k\pi : k \in Z\}.

\tan z := \frac {\sin z}{\cos z} \text { for } z \in \mathbb {C} \setminus \{\frac {\pi }{2} + k\pi : k \in \mathbb {Z} \} \ , and \cot z := \frac {\cos z}{\sin z} \text { for } z \in \mathbb {C} \setminus \{k\pi : k \in \mathbb {Z} \} \ .

Complex trigonometric functions obey the usual analogous identities as their areal counterparts. Sin and cos are also obviously holomorphic on the whole complex plane and their derivatives are analogous to the one's in real analysis.
The following could've been a definition of the \cos and \sin functions.

fr:title.text: Taylor series of cos and sin

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Taylor series of cos and sin

fr:mainmatter.html:p: For all z \in \mathbb {C} it holds \cos z = \sum \limits _{n=0}^{\infty } \frac {(-1)^n z^{2n}}{(2n)!} \ , \sin z = \sum \limits _{n=0}^{\infty } \frac {(-1)^n z^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}. Both of these series converge absolutely and uniformly.
We define \cosh z and \sinh z for all z \in \mathbb {C} with: \cosh z := \frac {1}{2}(e^{z} + e^{-z}), \sinh z := \frac {1}{2}(e^{z} - e^{-z}).
From the so far listed definitions, it's straightforward to see that \sin z = 1/i \sinh (iz) = -i \sinh (iz) and that \cos z = \cosh (iz).

html:ol.html:li: \sinh z and \cosh z are periodic of period 2\pi i.
\cosh z is even and \sinh z is odd.
For all z,w \in \mathbb {C} additive formulas hold.
\sinh z and \cosh z are holomorphic on \mathbb {C} and their derivatives are the usual ones.
For all z \in \mathbb {C} the equality holds \cosh ^2 z - \sinh ^2 z =1.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let us note here that x^2 - y^2 = 1 is the equation of the central unit hyperbola in the plane, that's where the "hyperbolic" comes from.
For example, the solutions of the equation \sinh z = 0 is the set \{k\pi i : k \in \mathbb {Z} \} and the set of solutions of \cosh z = 0 is \{\pi i /2 + k\pi i : k \in \mathbb {Z}\}.

\tanh z := \frac {\sinh z}{\cosh z}, \ z \in \mathbb {C} \setminus \{\pi i/2 + k\pi i : k \in \mathbb {Z}\}, \coth z := \frac {\cosh z}{\sinh z}, \ z \in \mathbb {C} \setminus \{k\pi i : k \in \mathbb {Z}\}.
